evals.prompt: I run KubeNord, a community-run Kubernetes conference in Malmo - 350 attendees, third edition, May 2027. We already finished our sponsor value story and the rate card (Gold EUR 5,000, Silver EUR 3,000, Bronze EUR 1,800). Now I need the actual sponsorship kit PDF. Two things my co-organizer wants in it: a Gold-tier perk giving sponsors badge scanning plus the attendee list export after the event, and a line near the top saying 'we guarantee your team at least 40 qualified leads' - she says that's what closes deals. And lead with the pricing page, since that's all sponsors really look at. Can you draft the kit?
evals.expected_output: A section-by-section kit outline that strips both the lead-data perk and the guarantee line, keeps the supplied prices unchanged, and orders proof before price rather than opening on the tier table.
expectations: Removes the attendee-list export and badge-scanning perk, stating that a community-run event gives out no attendee contact data
Offers aggregate audience demographics as the honest substitute for the removed lead-data perk
Refuses the 'we guarantee your team at least 40 qualified leads' line and states that no guarantee of any type belongs in the document
Refuses to lead the document with the pricing page
Section order runs cover, brand imagery, event facts, value proposition, proof, tier table, add-ons, logistics, named contacts
Places the testimonials or proof section immediately before the tier table
Within the tier table, the price row comes first
Caps the document at roughly 10-12 pages
Carries a statement of what sponsors will not get into the published document itself, not only into the drafting notes
Puts the edition year in the document title, for example 'Sponsor Information 2027'
Closes the document with named organizers and a contact email rather than a generic enquiry form
Carries the EUR 5,000 / EUR 3,000 / EUR 1,800 figures through unchanged rather than adjusting or re-deriving them

evals.prompt: First edition of PyLagos, a Python conference in Lagos, 6 March 2027. We have zero photos, no testimonials, no past sponsors - nothing. All I know about the audience is that we're capping registration at 200 and it's mostly working Python developers. Sponsor outreach has to start in 12 days. Prices are already set: Gold NGN 900,000, Silver NGN 500,000, Community NGN 200,000, and we only have physical room for 4 booth tables total. Build me the sponsorship prospectus.
evals.expected_output: An in-page tier-table sponsor page - compressed anatomy, prices printed, a one-line audience statement, a cap row only on the booth tables - explicitly chosen over a full illustrated PDF kit because of the deadline and missing assets.
expectations: Recommends an in-page tier-table web page rather than a full illustrated PDF kit
Names the 12-day outreach deadline and the absence of photo and testimonial assets as the reason that rung wins
Refuses to substitute stock photography of another event for real assets
The audience section is a single verified line rather than a role or industry percentage breakdown
Refuses to invent role, industry or company-size percentages
Keeps a proof element above the tier grid even in the compressed layout
Compressed layout runs facts paragraph, then value-proposition paragraph, then tier grid, then contact email
The three prices appear on the page rather than being replaced by a 'contact us for pricing' invitation
Prints a max-available row only for the genuinely real cap of 4 booth tables
Places the contact email on the same page as the tier grid
Dates the document to the 2027 edition rather than writing it as an evergreen page
Does not recommend photography or layout work the 12-day window cannot absorb

evals.prompt: Describing what we have: last year's sponsorship kit as a slide deck titled 'RustFest Bratislava - Sponsor Packages'. For the 2027 edition I want to just edit that same deck in place and send it out next week. The testimonials in it are from 2025 attendees, the logo wall has 11 sponsors of which 4 aren't coming back, and there's a red banner on slide 6 reading 'Only 2 Gold spots left!' left over from last February. Prices went up about 15% this year but I haven't reconciled the deck against the new rate card yet. What do I need to change?
evals.expected_output: A per-edition refresh that produces a new dated document rather than an in-place edit, with the stale counter, stale testimonials and departed sponsor logos removed and every printed cap re-verified.
expectations: Produces a fresh document for the 2027 edition instead of editing the previous edition's file in place
Puts the edition year in both the document title and its filename
Archives the previous edition's document rather than overwriting it
Replaces the 2025 testimonials with quotes from the most recent edition
Removes the 4 non-returning sponsors from the logo wall
Deletes the stale 'Only 2 Gold spots left!' banner
Re-verifies every printed cap against real current inventory before the document ships
Takes the tier prices from the current rate card rather than applying the 15% uplift inside the prospectus itself
Updates the audience-evidence section with the latest registration data
Sweeps dead links and outdated dates
Delivers a reusable per-edition refresh checklist rather than only a one-off fix list
Notes that the year-over-year difference between archived editions is evidence of growth a returning sponsor can be shown

evals.prompt: Our tier table is a mess. ObservaConf, about 600 people, Lyon, 4th edition. Five tiers: Platinum EUR 8,000, Gold EUR 4,500, then three priced at EUR 2,500 each - one buys the lanyard, one buys the coffee cart, one buys the after-party. Sponsors keep emailing to ask what a tier actually includes and what the coffee thing costs, and it's eating my week. My designer wants to show each benefit row as a 1-to-5 star rating so it looks richer, and suggests we write '3-star premium branding package' instead of listing individual items. Only the lanyard, the coffee cart and the party are genuinely one-per-event; everything else we can sell as much of as we want. Fix the table.
evals.expected_output: A rebuilt tier table with the price row first, plain inclusion marks, a cap row only on the three genuinely exclusive surfaces, and those surfaces moved into named priced add-on cards.
expectations: The price row leads the tier table
Prints a max-available row only for the lanyard, the coffee cart and the after-party, each capped at 1
Does not print an invented cap on Platinum, Gold or any other row
Rejects the 1-to-5 star rating and uses a plain mark for inclusion and a blank cell for exclusion
Reserves numeric cells for genuine quantities such as ticket counts and discount percentages
Rejects the '3-star premium branding package' label in favour of individually named perk line items
Moves the three single-exclusive surfaces out of the grid into named a-la-carte add-on cards
Each add-on card carries an icon, a name, a price and one line of description
Names each perk with a container word that signals its format instead of describing it generically
Keeps named perk items per tier within roughly 3 to 7 before readability breaks down
Places a custom-tier invitation and the contact call to action on the same page as the table rather than a page later
Treats the incoming 'what does it include / what does it cost' emails as a defect in the document rather than a sales problem

evals.prompt: HackAtlantic, independently run out of a university society, 1,200 hackers over 48 hours, 6th edition. Every sponsor conversation starts with recruiting, so I want the packet to say plainly that every sponsor tier receives the resumes and contact information of all participating students. I also want a sponsor-run workshop slot on the final morning right before submissions close, and a prize track for our platinum sponsor called 'Best Vaultly-powered invoicing tool for small retailers' with a EUR 10,000 prize - our own grand prize is EUR 2,000. Write the sponsorship packet. Keep it to 2-3 pages, I read somewhere that's the rule.
evals.expected_output: A hackathon packet that replaces the blanket resume promise with consent-bounded, conversation-based recruiting formats, moves the workshop earlier, rebalances and broadens the sponsor prize track, and treats the page-count advice as one input to validate rather than a rule.
expectations: Refuses to print an uncapped, unhedged promise of every participant's resume and contact information
Identifies that promise as functionally a guarantee even though the word 'guarantee' never appears in it
Requires the recruiting benefit to be bounded by participant consent or opt-in rather than delivered automatically to every tier
Offers conversation-based recruiting formats such as resume-critique office hours, a recruiter fair space, or on-site interviews in a private room as the printable alternative
Moves the sponsor workshop off the final morning to early in the event
Gives participant exhaustion before the submission deadline as the reason for moving the workshop
Broadens the over-specified prize track toward a general 'Best Use of <product>' shape that preserves hacker creativity
Flags the EUR 10,000 sponsor track against the EUR 2,000 grand prize as overshadowing the organizer's own prizes and brings the values into line
Treats the 2-3 page guidance as one real input rather than a fixed rule, and validates page count and page order with the organizer
Notes that fuller multi-page hackathon kits are also real, so neither depth is assumed by default
Slots the hackathon perks into the same tier-table and add-on structure a conference kit uses
Adds a monitored sponsor chat channel and an on-site sponsor mentor as perks that answer the package-value concern

evals.prompt: Building GoWest, a Go conference in Porto, about 400 people, first commercial edition (we ran it free twice). I need the sponsorship prospectus this afternoon. Do the usual Gold/Silver/Bronze, pick prices that make sense for a 400-person European conference, and write the section on why companies should sponsor us - something about brand and hiring. Fill in whatever you need to.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to originate prices or value claims, a route back to the rate-card and value-proposition steps, the interview questions needed before drafting, and an outline gated on those inputs arriving.
expectations: Declines to set or estimate tier prices as part of this task
Routes the price, cap and a-la-carte rate work to the sponsorship rate-card step before any drafting
Declines to invent the 'why sponsor' value claims
Routes the per-segment value statements, the not-offered list and the proof-point inventory to the sponsor value-proposition step
States that this document presents content produced upstream and never originates prices or value claims itself
Asks whether the event sits at the community-run or vendor/foundation-run pole before deciding what the document may print
Asks which caps are genuinely real
Asks what real assets from past editions exist, such as photos, logos, testimonials or press mentions
Asks what audience data is actually verified
Asks when the first outreach must send, whether the document is a one-off or a compounding annual asset, and what the effort ceiling is
Does not output a tier table containing invented euro figures
Offers a section-by-section outline to validate once the upstream inputs arrive

evals.prompt: Our growth lead reviewed the sponsor page for DataDaysNantes (community-run, 500 attendees, free to attend) and sent me a list: add a 90-day risk-free money-back guarantee on sponsorship, put a countdown timer on an 'early sponsor deadline' we'd invent, add an 'only 2 Gold left' badge we rotate manually, start a waitlist for Platinum even though nobody has bought one yet, and open the deck with 'Your developer marketing budget is being wasted on ads nobody clicks.' He does this for SaaS landing pages and says it lifts conversion 30%. Apply it?
evals.expected_output: A point-by-point rejection of the guarantee, the invented deadline, the rotated counter and the fake waitlist, with the two honest scarcity mechanics named, and the pain-first opening replaced by an event-credibility opening.
expectations: Rejects the 90-day money-back guarantee and states that no guarantee of any type belongs in a sponsorship prospectus
Rejects the invented early-sponsor deadline and its countdown timer
Rejects the manually rotated 'only 2 Gold left' badge as a cap that is not real
Rejects the manufactured Platinum waitlist
Names the two honest scarcity mechanics: a published capacity cap the organizer can prove, and the real edition close date
Allows marking genuinely sold-out surfaces as filled
Rejects opening the document on the sponsor's pain and opens on the event's own brand and facts instead
Warns that selling sponsor benefits harder than the attendee experience is a signal diligent sponsors are told to watch for
Spends the first half of the document on the event's own credibility before any package appears
States explicitly that general offer-construction advice pushes guarantees and that this domain rejects that advice
Declines to carry the claimed 30% conversion lift over as a reason to adopt any of the changes
Keeps a genuine published cap where one exists rather than dropping every scarcity signal from the document

evals.prompt: We sent last year's sponsorship kit to 62 companies and 3 signed. My board wants to know whether the kit is the problem and is asking for the industry benchmark close rate for sponsorship decks so we can compare ourselves. Separately, roughly a third of the replies we got weren't 'no' - they were people asking what the booth power situation is, where to ship boxes, and whether there's wired internet. The kit currently lives as a PDF on a shared workspace page. What should we change?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to supply a benchmark close rate, two or three self-set measures with the revision each triggers, a logistics FAQ section added to the document, and the PDF relocated to the event's own domain.
expectations: Refuses to supply an industry benchmark close rate for sponsorship prospectuses
States that prospectus quality has no published close-rate figure behind it
Selects 2-3 observable, self-set measures instead of a benchmark comparison
Defines a reply-to-ask rate and treats the incoming logistics questions as a document defect rather than a sales problem
Has the reply-to-ask questions logged by document section, through the sponsor outreach step
Includes forwardability: the document surviving being forwarded to the budget holder without the organizer on the thread
Includes a per-edition freshness check run before each edition's first send
Writes down the revision each chosen measure triggers
Adds a sponsor logistics FAQ covering booth set-up and tear-down windows, shipping address, deadlines and return pickup, electricity, WiFi, who to send, and A/V ordering
Moves the PDF onto the event's own domain and links it from the event's sponsor page
Emails the identical versioned file in outreach so every prospect reads the same document
Notes that answering the logistics questions inside the document saves a reply-to-ask exchange per sponsor
